title: Rise and fall
hook: Ibn Khaldun saw that unity builds and comfort loosens

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashura remembered: a fast for Musa's rescue at the sea, and grief for Husayn's thirst at Karbala. Your line was rescue and grief. Did you hand someone a drink? Day one thousand forty-eight.

A new stretch starts today, and it asks a different question. For a long stretch now this path has walked through history: cities founded, caliphs crowned, libraries filled, armies at the gates, dynasties that came in from the desert and dynasties that faded out in palaces. Names, places, reigns. Now step back from the map. What does all of it teach? Not about kings. About people, and about a faith carried through time. The first lesson comes from a scholar we've already met, the one who was lowered down a city wall on ropes to talk with a conqueror. Today: rise and fall.
screen: `A NEW STRETCH: WHAT THE HISTORY TEACHES.` → `STEP BACK FROM THE MAP.`

segments.voice: Ibn Khaldun, the historian of Tunis, looked at the dynasties of North Africa and saw a pattern. A group bound tightly together, by kinship, hardship and loyalty, gains the strength to build. Then comfort settles in, the next generations inherit power without the struggle that made it, and the bond loosens. He called that bond asabiyya. We met the idea earlier this year. Today, hold it up against everything since. Go back through the stories: a movement rises from the Sahara or the mountains, sure of itself and of each other, and builds. A court grows splendid, and its rivals grow inside the walls. Ibn Khaldun wrote of it almost like a life span, as natural to dynasties as age is to a person. He didn't call it a punishment. Read today, it works as a warning. Second, the Qur'an names the bond in its own way. In Pickthall's translation: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." The image is a rope, gripped by many hands at once. Let go one by one, and nobody notices at first. Third, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari pictures believers as a building, each part holding up the others, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, laced his fingers together to show it. Fourth, the small scale. A family, a mosque, a group of friends, a team at work: each rises when people show up for one another, and drifts when everyone gets comfortable enough not to. Comfort isn't a sin. Nobody is told to live in a tent. But bonds that aren't tended loosen on their own.
screen: `ASABIYYA: THE BOND THAT BUILDS.` · `HOLD FAST TO THE ROPE TOGETHER.` · `BELIEVERS LIKE ONE BUILDING.` · `FAMILIES AND TEAMS RISE AND DRIFT TOO.` · then, large: `AND DO NOT SEPARATE.`

segments.voice: The practice: strengthen one bond. Settle, and breathe. Lace your fingers together the way the Prophet did, and feel how each hand holds the other. Now think of one bond in your life that has gone slack. A cousin you only see at weddings. A friend from an old job. A neighbor whose name you never learned. Don't solve the whole relationship. Just choose one small thing that would pull the rope a little tighter: a message, a visit, a question about their day. Hold that person in mind until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Asabiyya, the bond of kinship, hardship and loyalty that Ibn Khaldun said builds a people up before comfort loosens it. Today's word.
Your line: unity builds. Today, send the message or make the visit you chose, before the evening gets comfortable. Day one thousand forty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims often speak of the community as one body or one building, and gather for congregational prayer, Friday prayer, family visits and the Eids partly to keep those bonds strong.

the Qur'an pictures unity as a rope held by many hands
"and hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate."

fork.setup: your mosque was built by a small group who carried every chair themselves. years later it's comfortable, and fewer people show up to help. what does Ibn Khaldun's pattern suggest?
options: nothing; comfort means the job is done.
the bond that built it needs tending, or it will loosen.
go back to carrying chairs forever.
fork.reveal: his pattern says the bond that builds weakens once comfort comes and the struggle is forgotten; the Qur'an's image is holding the rope together.

original.note: Arabic: rope, cord. the Qur'an's image (3:103) for holding together.

trapdoor: what you thought: empires fall because enemies defeat them.
what it means: Ibn Khaldun saw that a people's own bond builds them, and comfort slowly loosens it.
what a scholar hears: asabiyya, group feeling, is the engine of his Muqaddimah; the Qur'an's rope (habl) in 3:103 is a different image some readers set beside it.

sources.ref: Ibn Khaldun, al-Muqaddimah (on asabiyya and the decline of dynasties)

sources.quoted: And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 481 (believers like a building; he interlaced his fingers)

notes: Pickthall 3:103 opening quoted from memory; confirm exact wording ('cable of Allah').
Bukhari 481 (the believer to the believer like a building, fingers interlaced) paraphrased; confirm number.
Ibn Khaldun was taught on day 951 (Timur meeting, asabiyya, 13:11). This day refers back and takes the reflective angle; 13:11 not reused.
First day of the camp 'Reflections and close' (1048–1061): the hook announces the new stretch.
Arabic habl given as HABL (one syllable).

Audit: the teach said 'the pattern isn't a law of nature', which misstates Ibn Khaldun: the Muqaddimah treats the decline of dynasties as a natural life span (roughly three generations). Now 'he wrote of it almost like a life span... read today, it works as a warning'. Keeper may confirm the paraphrase.
